Hi! I'm Yusuf, a student at WE Applied Technology Schools with a strong interest in AI, data analysis, networking, cybersecurity, and space exploration.
I enjoy learning new technologies, solving problems, and turning creative ideas into practical projects. I'm currently working on LunarLens, an AI-assisted platform that aims to make lunar surface data easier to explore and understand.
I'm looking for motivated teammates.I believe different skills and perspectives can make our project stronger.
summary: Madar (Arabic for "orbit") is a browser game that lets Arabic-speaking kids design a space mission. Players pick a world (Moon, Venus, Mars or Europa), build a spacecraft within mass and budget limits, choose a launch day on an orbit diagram, then watch the flight and read a mission report with star ratings. A live drawing of the spacecraft updates as parts are added. Game rules follow facts published by NASA: Mars launch windows about every 26 months, Venus surface heat near 467 C, the long lunar night, and radiation near Europa. A failed mission explains why, so the player can fix the design and try again. The interface is in Egyptian Arabic and runs on a phone browser with no install or account. Code, text and SVG artwork were created with AI assistance (Claude) and reviewed by our team.
details: Challenge: Space Mission Design Game. What it does. Madar is a single-player game in Egyptian Arabic. The player chooses a destination (Moon, Venus, Mars, Europa), then designs a mission: rocket size, spacecraft type (orbiter, lander, rover), power source, antenna, science instruments, radiation or heat protection, and a landing system. A live spacecraft drawing and a parts list update as parts are chosen. For Venus, Mars and Europa the player picks a launch day on an orbit diagram. The flight plays out as a list of events (launch, cruise, entry, landing, surface work, sending data) and ends with a mission report, 1 to 3 stars, a mission patch and tips. What problem it solves. Space missions are decisions under limits, but most kids only see finished rockets. Madar lets them make those decisions and see the consequences, in their own language. Most space games for children are English only. What it teaches. Mass and budget limits; why launch timing matters; that sunlight is weaker far from the Sun so far missions need nuclear power; that signals take time and far missions send data slowly; that each world needs different design choices (no air on the Moon so parachutes fail; extreme heat on Venus; dust storms on Mars; radiation at Europa). Who it is for. School-age Arabic-speaking children, at home or in a class. This is our intended audience and has not yet been tested with children. How we built it. One HTML page with JavaScript, no server. Spacecraft, planets and the mission patch are drawn in code as SVG. A game engine models launch windows (transfer-orbit timing), solar power falling with the square of distance, light delay, mass/cost/power budgets, and landing and environment rules. An automated test tried about 50,000 designs per destination to tune difficulty so that good designs earn 3 stars and careless ones fail. A browser test clicked through the full game on phone and desktop sizes with no errors. Progress (best stars) is saved in the browser. Creativity. The player learns by designing and failing, not by reading. A launch-window helper, failure explanations and a live blueprint make the rules visible. Limitations (honest). Numbers are simplified for play and are not real mission data. NASA facts are used as written on NASA web pages; no live NASA datasets are connected. Tested in Chromium only. Not yet tested with children. Next steps. Test with students, add English, more destinations, and connect NASA open data.
